speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Good day.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This morning, the FOMC decided to maintain the target rate for the federal funds rate at 3¾ to 4 percent, in support of the Federal Reserve’s dual mandate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: While uncertainty remains—owing, in part, to geopolitical developments—domestic spending has been resilient.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Productivity growth is strong and capital investment robust.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But inflation remains elevated.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The Committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent goal.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The Committee will deliver price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: At each policy meeting, my colleagues and I assess the economy by looking out the window—it’s what we call “interrogating reality”—to gauge what’s really going on.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It is not a task that has grown easier.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Economic growth has strengthened.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The GDP increase in the first half of this year was revised up from an earlier estimate of 1.8 percent up to 2.4 percent.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And the third quarter appears to have brought an even more rapid advance, led by healthy consumer spending, likely running above 3 percent growth, and business investment—investment, likely rising at about a double-digit pace.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Capital expenditures are at a historically high share of GDP.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: High-tech investment is leading the acceleration.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But there’s also been a broadening in other categories.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And these trends bear watching.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The jobless rate is lower than a year ago, and payroll growth is noticeably above last year’s pace.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The four-week moving average of unemployment insurance claims continues to run at the lowest level in generations.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So on the employment side of the Fed’s dual mandate, conditions are quite positive.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And yet Americans, of course, are still dealing with inflation that has been running above the Committee’s objective for close to six years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s our responsibility to get inflation down.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s the reason the FOMC’s discussion over the last couple of days focused mainly on the price-stability side of our remit.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Since our policy action in September, we have started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They have tightened for some businesses and households, much as we would expect.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And while overall financial conditions are tighter, I’m unwilling and unable to call them “tight.” But broadly, these developments go in the direction of achieving a longer, more durable period of economic growth and price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Over the last couple of days, the Committee had a good discussion of the changes in the economic and financial landscape that marked this intermeeting period.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We discussed geopolitical developments and fast-moving changes in technology.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We observed, but were not surprised, that financial markets showed bouts of volatility and shifting correlations.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So as we widen the frame to survey the broad economic and financial picture, real activity is clearly pointing in the right direction.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s good news.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But inflation is too high.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out across the economy and that inflation expectations remain as they are—anchored.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: While these uncertainties are real, there’s no lack of clarity in our purpose at the Fed.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Since becoming Chairman just five months ago, I’ve been honored to work with FOMC policymakers who are unambiguous in their commitment to stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’ve made clear our readiness to act as circumstances require, and we have shown our willingness to act.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The information we receive over the coming period will help us determine where we want policy to be.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And at every turn, good or bad, our job is to get monetary policy right.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And that’s exactly what we’re doing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Now, with this objective in mind, we’ve decided on a change in our FOMC schedule, starting next fall.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We believe eight meetings per year is the right number for the FOMC.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But in 2027, one meeting will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The rest will be regular FOMC policy-setting meetings.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I expect that in 2028, we’ll have two meetings dedicated to discussions of strategy and six for setting policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: To me, it’s quite straightforward.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Getting policy right involves assessing near-term developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But it’s equally important we reserve time and space, as an intellectually diverse group, for strategic deliberations—for thinking anew about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons, focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I believe the setting of the meeting schedule and agenda is more than some administrative detail.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s an institutional choice, affecting the nature and the quality of our deliberations and, ultimately, the wisdom of our decisions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s yet another change to get the conduct of monetary policy on the right track.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I appreciate your attention this afternoon.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Now my time is yours, and I welcome your questions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So it’s a good question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I will say, I read your stories the last day or two, so I must admit I sort of saw that question coming.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I said in my prepared statement was information coming—in the coming period will help us tell us where we want to be, but I suspect you want a little more than that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So let me—let me give it a shot.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Ensuring price stability, Colby, quashing inflation is not about some fixed individual date on a calendar.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Same way it’s not about some isolated data point.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If it were about those two things, this job would be easier and we wouldn’t be suffering from nearly six years of inflation above target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s about ensuring we have clear objectives.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And it’s about a monetary policy strategy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Which might sound—to your ear, and others’—like a change from the last several years.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So let me step back.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: First thing we did when we showed up, with my colleagues, is we doubled down on the 2 percent inflation target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We said: “We own it, we’re taking responsibility for it, and if you think that we’re tolerating some inflation target somewhere in the 2s, let us disabuse you of it.” That was the first part of this new monetary medicine.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Second part is, we took responsibility: no “anguish of central banking” here, no blaming others.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So the third thing that we’ve done—we laid out for you and the world our framework.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I did it in Jackson Hole.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It was part of the discussion the last couple of days.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It is the framework that many of my colleagues hew to as well.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: This is how we think about how monetary policy should work.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: These are the transmission mechanisms.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And this is how we’re going to deliver.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We interrogate reality.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We do that periodically.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s a very useful thing to do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But we don’t just talk—we act.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And so in September when we last met, we acted.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We removed a dose of accommodation.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Inflation compensation as measured by swaps prices, many other measures—inflation compensation is going in the right way.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Inflation expectations—the world is quite unsettled.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They might have gone the wrong way.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They’ve gone the right way, too.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I feel good about those signposts.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The period right in front of us is information rich.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There is a lot that’s happening in the world.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’re going to be able to figure out what’s the appropriate protocol as part of this package that we started to deliver five months ago to deliver price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m encouraged by the progress we’ve made in a short period of time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But if the crux of your question is, “you haven’t delivered yet; you haven’t achieved price stability,” you’re right about that—but we’re working on it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Well, we’ve got to determine the appropriate protocol.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus, the overwhelming judgment is that what we’ve done in this monetary medicine is starting to work some, but there’s no firm conclusions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we’d announce it to much fanfare today.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What we decided to do was—to Colby’s question—take stock of where we are, evaluate what we’re seeing out the window, ask ourselves whether the period right in front of us is likely to provide more clarity on the appropriate protocol.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: My judgment, the judgment of my overwhelming number of colleagues, is that it would.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Those are two questions.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I would—that was like a parliamentary procedure question you were asking.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That didn’t count.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I hesitate to indulge the second question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I fear what it would do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: [Laughter] But let’s—let me see if I can do it and not have a slippery slope among us.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Your first question was about my colleagues.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’ve got 18 quite independent colleagues.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: If you were inside of that room the last couple of days, you would come to believe that to be true.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: One way to test the independence of my colleagues is—I don’t know if you’ve heard, Steve, but I don’t submit a dot.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t plan on submitting a dot, but the 18 of them do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: To suggest somehow that I am some kind of all-knowing person sending messages out, that, that’s not the Committee of the FOMC that I know.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: These are serious, sober, responsible people.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We had a serious, sober discussion.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So that’s the answer to that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: On the parliamentary question—which doesn’t count as a question—I’ll just say this: We’ve made a decision that, at that strategy meeting in ’27 and the two strategy meetings in ’28, I do not anticipate making any policy decision, putting out a policy statement.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’s not obvious yet.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There’s more news to come on that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The decision on the new format for the meetings is relatively new.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It was a robust discussion over a couple of meetings of how to handle that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: As we get details of that, which are still now not until next fall, we’ll be prepared to share them with you.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So the mandate was given to us by Congress.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: The mandate was: Deliver stable prices and deliver full employment, all in the context of financial stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Now, they gave us some other homework to do on supervision and regulation and payments, but I presume you’re talking about monetary policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Ensure stable prices.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I mentioned, I think at a prior press conference, if you were trying to do the most harm to the least well-off among us, you would let the last six years of inflation above the Fed’s target—usually well above the Fed’s target—you’d let that continue.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So that’s the most important thing we can do as we look out the window.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And that’s what we plan to do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You probably heard me say this: We will deliver price stability—no ifs, ands, or buts.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And that continues to be the case.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Sure.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: These five task forces are hard at work.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I have scarcely seen anything that would constitute a final report.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I have done some periodic check-ins with them, and I am impressed by the rigor of the intellectual discussions, by the seriousness of the task that we’ve given them.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Now, some of the questions that I asked to kick off the reports, they want to answer those and answer a whole range of other questions, which might go to other task forces, but I’m impressed by what they’re doing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I gave them, like I told you, a year-end deadline.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think some, but not all, of the groups will probably hit their deadline and turn their homework in on time.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But that just begins the process by which we’re going to be consuming, which is intellectually serious work.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That’s a catalyst for us to think anew about productivity and jobs and an inflation framework and what’s the best data to help us do our job—how to think about the Balance Sheet Task Force.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: These are huge intellectual investments that I think are going to bear fruits in the next policy conjuncture—unlikely to find their way into this policy conjuncture given the, the important role as consumers of these ideas that my colleagues have.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I will have one small announcement.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I previewed this when I was at an IMF meeting, much to the chagrin of some of my colleagues around here.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: On November 16th, the Productivity and Jobs Task Force will be doing a field hearing, inviting a broad range of people who have strong views.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I know I, for one, am keenly interested in refining my own views on that question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But that task force decided that they wanted to hear from more people as part of their undertaking.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I plan on attending.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I might have a few words to say at the outset of that conference.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I expect the conference will go three or four hours.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It’ll be pretty wonky stuff.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t know how good the material will be for the likes of you and your colleagues.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But it’s a purpose to do a lot of listening—for me to interrogate the reality in front of me.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So we’re going to explore those largely in the public realm on November 16th.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I look forward to seeing you there.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, James, I appreciate the question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m not going to be responding to, to quotes from public officials.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: What I can tell you is my experience in five months here.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We just came out of a heck of a family fight—a serious, sober discussion.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think we came to the right policy decision for this moment, and I’m honored to be here and honored to be the Chairman of this group.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Yeah, so what I can do is tell you there’s no soft inflation target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There’s no implicit inflation target.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There’s a target of price stability, and it’s 2 percent as measured by PCE.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: It took six years to—for inflation to have the effect on consumers that you reference.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I would say this: When consumers interrogate reality, they look outside their window, too.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They go to the gas station, too.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And they see that prices are up.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I am not going to be the guy who says that oil prices haven’t gone up, and when they fill up their tank, they don’t see it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And so inflation’s gone up and expectations in the very near term, because they’re doing what we’re doing—interrogating reality.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But if you look out over the horizon, if you look at most, but not all, measures, what you see is households, businesses, financial markets, they have the confidence that they should have that the central bank will deliver price stability.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I don’t want to engage in hypotheticals, but I can look out—look out our window and see what’s happened.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: There’s been a stable correlation between oil prices as they’ve moved up this year, generally, and interest rates—not the interest rates that we control but interest rates set in the market.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: That correlation has been quite strong until very recently, where you’ve seen oil prices continue to move up, largely due to geopolitical events.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: We’ve seen crack spreads between oil and refined products continue to stay elevated.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Interest rates have rolled over to the downside.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I’m not a Wall Street newsletter; I’m just telling you, when I look out the window over the last several months, that is what we’ve seen.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: To the extent that oil prices were to move lower—again, probably due to geopolitical events—that’s something that we’re going to have to interrogate.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But that’s a hypothetical, and, in fact, if we look at financial market prices, futures prices for oil, they’ve moved up over the course of the last several weeks, and I can’t help but take note of that, too.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Thank you, Claire.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So there was a narrative for quite a while, maybe even in this room, over the course of the last several press conferences: “Well, they’re going to raise rates.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They’re talking about raising rates, but it’s not going to have any effect on AI because the returns that investors are expecting are so different.” I was skeptical of that view.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Interest rates get in the cracks.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Interest rates affect, directly or indirectly, almost everything.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Interest rates have had an effect.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You’ve seen market participants that are discriminating between the kinds of investments they want to make.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: You’ve seen credit spreads for certain assets widen out, gap out.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: For others, you’ve seen some tightening in financial conditions but not significantly.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I believe they do.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I don’t believe that they’re somehow divorced from the rest of the economy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Secondly, I’ll just say this: It is convenient to say that the strength of the economy is all about this new technology wave.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: In fact, if we look at the data, really including data from the last meeting until this, the cap-ex story is not just robust, not just strong, but it is broadening.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And so if you wanted to tell the story somehow that this is strength we’re seeing only in narrow pockets, that’s a much harder story to tell now than it would have been several quarters ago.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So politics played no role in the decision.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I didn’t hear an utterance about politics.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I didn’t hear a reference to politics, elections, what’s happening in the next week or so.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I didn’t hear anything about it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I don’t believe it had any role in the decision, not just for me, but my colleagues around the room.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But I will say, it’s an information-rich interval in the coming period, having nothing to do with politics.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So the blackout period for them ends, I think, on Friday or at some point over the weekend, so they might—they might indulge you in that discussion.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t believe in forward guidance, absent exigent circumstances, absent a crisis.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I have to give that caveat because in the darkest days of the 2008 financial crisis, in part using some literature and thinking from a very recent Nobel Prize winner, that kind of forward guidance is actually quite helpful.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But in normal, ordinary times, especially times where the underlying real economy is this strong, I don’t believe in it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t favor it.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I also don’t believe in prejudging meetings.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: A lot of things can happen.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I’m not going to be able to, to share with you my musings about what happens when this group gets together six weeks from now.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: But my judgment is that we might learn a lot and, like in my response to Colby’s question, we’ll be, I think, better positioned to determine the right policy decision and the stance of policy.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So, thank you for your question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: First off, I would say, I pay probably more attention to the Korean economy than you might think because when I’m looking at the feedstocks effectively for this new surge in technology, a lot of it’s coming from Japan and Korea, some from Singapore.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I’m particularly interested in, in what’s happening in the Korean economy, usually because it’s telling me what’s on planes and ships coming this way.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Secondly, I should say that your new central bank governor is someone I’ve known for 20 years and is a very talented guy and a good friend.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So I’m glad he’s in that post.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: He and I met actually about 20 years ago amid the Global Financial Crisis, as it would come to be known, and I remember—this is a generation ago—discussions with him about the use of the balance sheet in exigent circumstances like we had then.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: At this point, the balance sheet is solely within the four walls of the Balance Sheet Task Force.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Now I have checked in with them, full disclosure.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: They’re working away and comparing their best thoughts.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And I think the conclusions they come to, the recommendations they come to, will be fed into the FOMC probably early in the first quarter, but don’t hold me exactly to that timing.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: And, and if we decide to make changes in the balance sheet, it’ll be after a serious consideration of their proposals and their recommendations.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I think it is unlikely to have any material effect on this policy conjuncture, but it’s a question we should get to the bottom to, and I look forward to doing it with the help of the outside task force.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So you gave me two questions, and neither of them were—had any sort of parliamentary out.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: So you’re giving me the opportunity to choose, choose, choose which of those— NICK TIMIRAOS.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Fair enough.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: —so I’ll answer your second question.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: When we removed a dose of accommodation, I don’t know, six weeks ago—we don’t have perfect foresight on what financial markets are going to do with it—but broadly I would say, the effects on financial markets, on financial market conditions broadly, were consistent with my expectations.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Okay.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Give it to me again.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: I don’t remember.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
sentence: Good, good, good, good—good pickup of that.

speaker: CHAIRMAN WARSH
